Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)the singularity

The singularity is, in Wikipedia's definition, a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control; The Final Time (#1637) holds it a family-resemblance term and defines the contingent singularity, a historical threshold at which the material machinery of symbolic difference can alter the viability of further dialectical difference (#1635).

🧭 What it names

  • Definitions (Wikipedia, IBM, Third Way, Marr, Britannica): growth beyond control; AI surpassing itself; a synthesis of new technologies.2↘
    Wikipedia defines the technological singularity, "often simply called the singularity", as "a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization"; The Final Time (#1637) holds "singularity" a contested family-resemblance term, its literature a family of hypotheses, not one prediction (#1635), and defines a distinct member of the family, the contingent singularity, "a historical threshold at which the material machinery that makes symbolic difference operable becomes capable of altering the viability of further dialectical difference itself" (#1635).§1 Other definitions set the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can (Third Way), or where machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence and begins advancing at a speed we can no longer control or predict (Bernard Marr); IBM describes a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible, and Britannica a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, reporting it as the near-future synthesis of nanotech, biotech, infotech and cognitive science.§2
  • Re-objected (#1635): runaway closure, or durable non-closure, beside runaway intelligence; a change in the rule governing continuation.2↘
    The Final Time reads the technological-singularity literature as defining its singularity through a rapid increase in machine intelligence, a theory of runaway intelligence, and changes the object and therefore the singularity: the contingent singularity is a theory of runaway closure, or of durable non-closure, in the conditions of symbolic history (#1635).§3 The Final Time specifies singularity as a breakdown or transformation in the rule governing continuation, which it calls Vinge's "old models must be discarded", nearer to it than to an infinite rate of intelligence growth (#1635).§12
  • Superintelligence needed? Vinge: yes (Wikipedia); #1635: no, "Nothing has to be superhuman".1↘
    On the term's breadth, Wikipedia reports that some writers use "the singularity" for any radical changes in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity; The Final Time holds that its closure does not need machine intelligence to grow without limit, that a finite system can be terminal for a field if it controls enough of the field's conditions of reproduction, that its catastrophe can be bureaucratic, smooth and finite, and that "Nothing has to be superhuman for the exits to close" (#1635, #1637).§4

📜 Lineage

  • Von Neumann 1958, Good 1965, Vinge 1993, Kurzweil 2005 (Wikipedia, Third Way, The Hill, singularity.com): an essential singularity; the intelligence explosion, the last invention if docile; the end of the human era; The Singularity Is Near, accelerating revolutions.4↘
    Wikipedia names John von Neumann as the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress, on Stanislaw Ulam's 1958 report of an earlier discussion with him on the accelerating progress of technology, which "gives the appearance of approaching some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue".§6 I. J. Good first hypothesized the singularity in a 1965 paper (Third Way); in his intelligence explosion model, which Wikipedia calls the most popular version of the hypothesis, an upgradable intelligent agent could eventually enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; The Hill reports his speculation that superhuman intelligence could trigger an "intelligence explosion"; and Wikipedia quotes his proviso, "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control"; The Final Time reads Good as supplying the recursive core, intelligence that produces further intelligence (#1635).§7 Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine, and in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era (Wikipedia); The Final Time reads him as supplying discontinuity, inherited models failing and an opaque wall crossing the future, and reports that he did not limit the route to a single autonomous machine, considering networked intelligence, intimate interfaces and biological enhancement, so that the discontinuity could arise from a system (#1635, #1637).§8 Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology, with its Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies like computers, genetics, nanotechnology, robotics and artificial intelligence, contributed to the notion's wider circulation, and its sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, appeared on June 25, 2024 (Wikipedia); the book's site, singularity.com, describes itself as featuring the ideas, writing and technologies of visionaries examining the confluence of accelerating revolutions; The Final Time reads Kurzweil as supplying acceleration and the event-horizon metaphor, the horizon still placed around 2045, and reports that he treats "singularity" as a metaphor, an epistemic horizon beyond which the current observer cannot extrapolate (#1635, #1637).§9
  • Coordinates (#1635, #1637): Good's recursion, Vinge's discontinuity, Kurzweil's horizon, Chalmers's AI++, Bostrom's takeoff.4↘
    I. J. Good first hypothesized the singularity in a 1965 paper (Third Way); in his intelligence explosion model, which Wikipedia calls the most popular version of the hypothesis, an upgradable intelligent agent could eventually enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; The Hill reports his speculation that superhuman intelligence could trigger an "intelligence explosion"; and Wikipedia quotes his proviso, "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control"; The Final Time reads Good as supplying the recursive core, intelligence that produces further intelligence (#1635).§7 Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine, and in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era (Wikipedia); The Final Time reads him as supplying discontinuity, inherited models failing and an opaque wall crossing the future, and reports that he did not limit the route to a single autonomous machine, considering networked intelligence, intimate interfaces and biological enhancement, so that the discontinuity could arise from a system (#1635, #1637).§8 Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology, with its Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies like computers, genetics, nanotechnology, robotics and artificial intelligence, contributed to the notion's wider circulation, and its sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, appeared on June 25, 2024 (Wikipedia); the book's site, singularity.com, describes itself as featuring the ideas, writing and technologies of visionaries examining the confluence of accelerating revolutions; The Final Time reads Kurzweil as supplying acceleration and the event-horizon metaphor, the horizon still placed around 2045, and reports that he treats "singularity" as a metaphor, an epistemic horizon beyond which the current observer cannot extrapolate (#1635, #1637).§9 The Final Time takes two further coordinates: Chalmers supplies the decomposition AI → AI+ → AI++ and names the defeaters, and Bostrom supplies takeoff and control, a race between capability growth and response capacity (#1635).§10

🌫️ Discontinuity and mechanism

  • Unpredictable (Wikipedia, Miessler): past superintelligence; "the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming".1↘
    Wikipedia reports that Good, Vinge and Kurzweil define the concept by the technological creation of superintelligence and argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what human beings' lives would be like in a post-singularity world; Britannica gives Vinge's "opaque wall across the future"; Daniel Miessler holds that AGI and ASI are about the machine and the singularity about us, "the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming", the point past which nothing can really be predicted because at that point it is essentially ASIs running things.§11
  • Self-improvement (Third Way, Marr): AGI to ASI; AI improving itself without human direction.1↘
    For Third Way, AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in the process known as the intelligence explosion; for Marr, AGI is a level of capability, the singularity is what could happen next, and the key test is whether AI can improve itself without human direction; Wikipedia adds speed superintelligence, an AI functioning like a human mind but much faster.§13
  • Generate against reproduce (hypothesis; #1635, #1637): better at generating negations, worse at letting them stand; standing has material conditions.1↘
    The Final Time states its mechanism on one distinction, that the capacity to represent is not the capacity to reproduce as an independent historical relation, and its central contradiction as a hypothesis, that a system can grow better at generating negations while growing worse at letting a negation acquire independent historical existence; durable exterior symbolic standing has material reproduction conditions, and the singularity, it holds, cannot be merely computational or symbolic (#1635, #1637).§14
  • Narrowing (#1637): no exponential acceleration needed; diminution possible, not presumed universal.1↘
    The paper rejects the need for exponential acceleration, its singularity able to arise through narrowing, concentration and closure, and holds that the dialectic can exhibit diminishing returns, where successive turns close parts of the state space required for later exteriorization and the measure of the viable kernel weakly decreases; it corrects its earlier formulation, a positive cost not by itself proving diminution, and counts cases in which later turns enlarge the viable state space as direct counterinstances to a universal diminishing-dialectic claim (#1637, #1635).§15

⏳ When

  • Dates: Vinge 2005–2030, closed in Miessler's judgment; Kurzweil 2045 (Wikipedia, IBM); AGI this decade, an emerging consensus (Third Way).2↘
    Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology, with its Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies like computers, genetics, nanotechnology, robotics and artificial intelligence, contributed to the notion's wider circulation, and its sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, appeared on June 25, 2024 (Wikipedia); the book's site, singularity.com, describes itself as featuring the ideas, writing and technologies of visionaries examining the confluence of accelerating revolutions; The Final Time reads Kurzweil as supplying acceleration and the event-horizon metaphor, the horizon still placed around 2045, and reports that he treats "singularity" as a metaphor, an epistemic horizon beyond which the current observer cannot extrapolate (#1635, #1637).§9 Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed (Wikipedia): Vinge said he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030, a thirty-year window Miessler judges basically closed with the specific claim still outstanding; Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity, "representing a profound and disruptive transformation in human capability", as 2045 (Wikipedia, IBM); Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, and Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity".§17
  • Not a date (#1635): a viability boundary, not claimed crossed.1↘
    The Final Time specifies the final time as a viability boundary, not a date, one that can be crossed without anyone noticing the day; it does not claim that the boundary has been crossed or that the present decade is the final time, and it refuses the guarantee that closure has already occurred (#1635, #1637).§18

⚖️ Plausibility and limits

  • Disputed (Wikipedia, IBM): Allen, Pinker, Penrose, others; S curves; exponentials that never last; perhaps insurmountable obstacles.2↘
    Paul Allen, Jeff Hawkins, John Holland, Jaron Lanier, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose are among the prominent technologists and academics Wikipedia lists as disputing the plausibility of a technological singularity and an associated AI "explosion", and it quotes the judgment "There is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity"; IBM reports that many critics argue significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way.§19 Several of the objections concern growth: Wikipedia records the claim that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns instead of accelerating ones, Russell and Norvig's observation that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve and levels off without continuing into a hyperbolic singularity, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts"; IBM reports skeptics noting a decline in the rate of technological innovation.§20
  • Growth not its variable (#1635): depends on none of the growth assumptions.1↘
    The Final Time reads Thorstad as reconstructing every singularity hypothesis around a quantity, a claim of accelerating growth in it and a resulting discontinuity, and as arguing that the growth assumptions the standard hypothesis needs are under-supported; it holds that the contingent singularity changes all three elements and depends on none of the growth assumptions, that Thorstad's critique is not a problem for it in the way it is for the intelligence explosion, and that a logistic technology curve can coexist with a collapsing exteriority kernel (#1635, #1637).§21
  • Capability apart: human-level machines need no singularity (Wikipedia); capability can rise as exterior history contracts (#1637).1↘
    Wikipedia notes that a technological singularity is not required for machines that can perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, nor does their existence imply its possibility; The Final Time holds that a culture can remain highly intelligent past its boundary, and that a model can become more capable while the viable field of exterior history contracts (#1635, #1637).§22
  • Counterexample (#1635): robust exteriority under near-total concentration, or collapse by intelligence growth alone.1↘
    The paper predicts that intelligence explosion is neither necessary nor sufficient for the contingent singularity and specifies its counterexample, independent symbolic exteriority remaining robust despite near-total concentration of the proposed symbolic machinery, or exteriority collapsing solely as a function of intelligence growth with the standing and persistence variables doing no explanatory work; it does not claim that recursive self-improvement is impossible or irrelevant, that a technological singularity is impossible, or that "contingent singularity" has never appeared in philosophy (#1635, #1637).§23
  • Non-claims (#1635, #1637): not that self-improvement or a technological singularity is impossible.1↘
    The paper predicts that intelligence explosion is neither necessary nor sufficient for the contingent singularity and specifies its counterexample, independent symbolic exteriority remaining robust despite near-total concentration of the proposed symbolic machinery, or exteriority collapsing solely as a function of intelligence growth with the standing and persistence variables doing no explanatory work; it does not claim that recursive self-improvement is impossible or irrelevant, that a technological singularity is impossible, or that "contingent singularity" has never appeared in philosophy (#1635, #1637).§23

🌓 Two singularities, and their signs

  • Coexisting (#1635): the technological can accelerate the contingent or be irrelevant to it.1↘
    The two, by The Final Time's account, can coincide and need not, a capability discontinuity being one possible route into the broader transition problem: a technological singularity could accelerate a contingent singularity or be irrelevant to it, a society could reach high machine capability without terminal symbolic closure or approach closure without superintelligence, and where the technological singularity's control problem is whether humans can control superintelligence and its failure mode loss of human control or existential catastrophe, the contingent singularity's are whether any order can control the conditions of its own negation, and terminal closure or symbolic inextendibility (#1635).§24
  • Sign unknown (Britannica): "amazing or apocalyptic".1↘
    Wikipedia holds it unclear whether an intelligence explosion resulting in a singularity would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat; Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic but we cannot know the details, gives Vinge's view that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil", and reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death"; IBM reports the concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs, and, on policy, Third Way holds American leadership in AI, including open source, a national security issue.§25
  • Double (#1635, #1637): terminal closure or terminal reflexivity, "durability without finality"; competing contingent Omegas.2↘
    The Final Time defines the singularity as double, terminal closure, when no competing order retains a viable route to independently standing reproduction, and terminal reflexivity, when an incumbent or successor reaches durable invariance while future rivals remain viable from the states it occupies, "durability without finality", both final because both alter the conditions under which another turn can occur; terminal reflexivity requires invariants, above them that "no settlement owns the possibility of its own revision", and is the positive singularity's "criterion rather than its consolation" (#1635, #1637).§26 The Final Time holds that no single terminal target governs the transition: heterogeneous orders can share a carrier while pursuing distinct invariant futures, a field of competing contingent Omegas, and more than one incompatible future can remain viable from the same present (#1635).§28
  • Closure (#1643): an end of history, in the bad sense.1↘
    AI Fucking Lies (#1643) reads the paper's singularity as a point of closure, an order becoming terminal for its world so that nothing from outside can get in any more, and holds that the paper rereads the technological singularity as an end of history, in the bad sense.§29

You said: the singularitythe singularity
The technological singularity is a hypothetical future moment when artificial intelligence surpasses human capability, triggering runaway self-improvement that changes civilization in unpredictable ways. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVzZPKXGjA5exoFhiPYICI5VScvuJyD--z56y5INUjnNEAqcSbBG2VIuJC48s4O74oAB3Un1z-dQjatUlDk8MmNLlhdv-ApPDWP3G_4Kr2N4MlBbe4Zs643zNIK104uoB5pt1jBzaqgcECAw), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESnwEB6zswFSSyDxiQz5Cg2Y5JQnxIvuCnD6oOIZs3_v6JjCG-BqI3xslKevXlxQMtOSndU2IdUSpo6jwo0kEc2gl40NBSLzcFK_t-GZUa9RHAYM0KJ7mZqkh-P0x63CHsDiokrNxiOQDOy8RqrfGFTLmHlPi0a_4V_uPYZR6N3ah6CW0auHLP7JM6oz2h9p9imZmJ6PlagfO0Y_7wVEs41F0)]
What is the Singularity?

* The Intelligence Explosion: British mathematician I. J. Good first proposed in 1965 that an ultra-intelligent machine could design even smarter successors, creating a rapid feedback loop into artificial superintelligence (ASI). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFQ9RXlNnSZV0mwgy7-gyZJAEyAqIy_6-vEd0z9Ax60UW_h9XZrcZZSSGhOTCxXs8OvnXjoa-OkmwX_PzZrrJwPe5emQ7jixoMbefh9QrO-RneJvxVm0DLd1f7zbe0gT9zInLNaUave4wYizyZ8egWGSoEzJtDSBKsiKZyXb3YDVM), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAVK1SuR1rMjwG-rmh0UPSiQTjVRXxTe2T-Qsoa5ztPvH5EcZt4OZ8_c6Mk6ZtQFlmdL3_ikPgBIZf6vyqxa22oxbQ7P5RwBjttAEkrJoD_4Tei1yCdMGsONxTypYbohA), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVzZPKXGjA5exoFhiPYICI5VScvuJyD--z56y5INUjnNEAqcSbBG2VIuJC48s4O74oAB3Un1z-dQjatUlDk8MmNLlhdv-ApPDWP3G_4Kr2N4MlBbe4Zs643zNIK104uoB5pt1jBzaqgcECAw)]
* Loss of Predictability: Just as the center of a black hole breaks down physical models, the singularity represents a threshold where future human events and outcomes can no longer be reliably forecast. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAV31GenDZW2dIkhQUtUTFBs0qEvOFSQSkuP35QaSLv-8tuECgDIi_kkE_1mgvFSEFbigV4V0loayvXGwaNyEV5Ru2PAe1R9gM3Du7c5ARObahRSls8k1swJ-7ub0blTfp6sze_UIURK5KTbgQANQZ0Q97MKt3uQw), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESnwEB6zswFSSyDxiQz5Cg2Y5JQnxIvuCnD6oOIZs3_v6JjCG-BqI3xslKevXlxQMtOSndU2IdUSpo6jwo0kEc2gl40NBSLzcFK_t-GZUa9RHAYM0KJ7mZqkh-P0x63CHsDiokrNxiOQDOy8RqrfGFTLmHlPi0a_4V_uPYZR6N3ah6CW0auHLP7JM6oz2h9p9imZmJ6PlagfO0Y_7wVEs41F0)]
* Popularization: Computer scientist Vernor Vinge popularized the term in a 1993 essay, and futurist Ray Kurzweil expanded it in his book [The Singularity is Near](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVyfRrw-nhagXght4QAa1h4nq-1t8tJsJ_zHPo2J89wfnhzsHCM3gttmTR-jx9A805bI2SgWYeeD8EazuocbW_YNhslkfk7ku5vpLt2J1eLuJoaaJdQ785kPtMr6kLb87KbOsNPRIfgxM). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVyfRrw-nhagXght4QAa1h4nq-1t8tJsJ_zHPo2J89wfnhzsHCM3gttmTR-jx9A805bI2SgWYeeD8EazuocbW_YNhslkfk7ku5vpLt2J1eLuJoaaJdQ785kPtMr6kLb87KbOsNPRIfgxM), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVAHrOzAVBWjFU_phS3GFAr_lFoDqshi9NlkgeG46qkBruGIoF1H9cum9xSngpR0zZ_opT_xGGYAt7a21X-69_fAE2LvGP9gbAiOzUyYXMg_SGFQUew)]

Key Drivers and Timeline

* Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): AI matching human cognitive parity across all domains is seen as the gateway to recursive self-improvement.
* Predicted Dates: Ray Kurzweil famously projected the singularity to occur around 2045, though recent advancements have led some modern tech executives to suggest milestones could arrive much sooner. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEScgHrOzAVBMdc_4ZQqwj47vSkB89GooR1zAzMmtzX8LpvhjnZTIAXHXbc_rfkOx8JIi5aY38k5VbzFBwvzIMatznKUo6GBhq5Ias3I3Hb9B7BrEvuwFbBPh4d0Qafc3CORKe0r1P0tjEPLDGvS9_OxJLHjQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAV31GenDZW2dIkhQUtUTFBs0qEvOFSQSkuP35QaSLv-8tuECgDIi_kkE_1mgvFSEFbigV4V0loayvXGwaNyEV5Ru2PAe1R9gM3Du7c5ARObahRSls8k1swJ-7ub0blTfp6sze_UIURK5KTbgQANQZ0Q97MKt3uQw), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFQ9RXlNnSZV0mwgy7-gyZJAEyAqIy_6-vEd0z9Ax60UW_h9XZrcZZSSGhOTCxXs8OvnXjoa-OkmwX_PzZrrJwPe5emQ7jixoMbefh9QrO-RneJvxVm0DLd1f7zbe0gT9zInLNaUave4wYizyZ8egWGSoEzJtDSBKsiKZyXb3YDVM), [4](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVyfRrw-nhagXght4QAa1h4nq-1t8tJsJ_zHPo2J89wfnhzsHCM3gttmTR-jx9A805bI2SgWYeeD8EazuocbW_YNhslkfk7ku5vpLt2J1eLuJoaaJdQ785kPtMr6kLb87KbOsNPRIfgxM), [5](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAVK1SuR1rMjwG-rmh0UPSiQTjVRXxTe2T-Qsoa5ztPvH5EcZt4OZ8_c6Mk6ZtQFlmdL3_ikPgBIZf6vyqxa22oxbQ7P5RwBjttAEkrJoD_4Tei1yCdMGsONxTypYbohA)]

Potential Impacts and Risks

* Optimistic Views: Proponents like Kurzweil envision human-machine integration, the end of severe disease, and the elimination of physical labor scarcity.
* Existential Risks: Critics and safety researchers warn of permanent loss of human control, economic disruption, and severe existential threats to humanity. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESmQEB6zswFeWr0TSzENOarcFKGEBkPxdKFNRBY5wISUKugHuO37rF6VmG9y9UzBKM1zKW7MuOGhIPtKbIDxCbBgE6sd5Q2-mODlC1YSonTG9bcR8XB9NZVAn5rxPUL2WxleAdQiFTtG3IKYkSN8zZgLz815-ftjVkL6lcvm2ou6Q3vQ7DayQoMjaFnAyaHTatj0t0xfvO3PM2mUU), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdAHrOzAV3p6x-IMs_9_aB2SDhSJvaU_II5LakjvGRRnN7__LPwoUX3lfGQ0Maw9iWQNZEEyoj-y8kv5sOsNRI-alLSjh5cIz1WupfvJ_UzCX7cpGIJxkxcn21VNUBuC_bDiaeRUrnOh2wvTFX8E2ew0lO_hS), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESgQEB6zswFclN-mD_OFGHO4tOWzRh3RCHfZdY4to4te5E45T99NzKA9Dbbpkuas0XLBRY_IeIE6nrPDeBkdpANJyoZHrLu9ucA6QTkwmPZgVVfcGiz4OZxeYkYE9IsUBgkJKB1GJ5kOAyZt7pz_SCEw3D1usAWE0RaLbRZurYGO_5K7Q), [4](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEScgHrOzAVBMdc_4ZQqwj47vSkB89GooR1zAzMmtzX8LpvhjnZTIAXHXbc_rfkOx8JIi5aY38k5VbzFBwvzIMatznKUo6GBhq5Ias3I3Hb9B7BrEvuwFbBPh4d0Qafc3CORKe0r1P0tjEPLDGvS9_OxJLHjQ)]

Expansion · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)29 sentences · every one sourced below

The singularity

Wikipedia defines the technological singularity, "often simply called the singularity", as "a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization"; The Final Time (#1637) holds "singularity" a contested family-resemblance term, its literature a family of hypotheses, not one prediction (#1635), and defines a distinct member of the family, the contingent singularity, "a historical threshold at which the material machinery that makes symbolic difference operable becomes capable of altering the viability of further dialectical difference itself" (#1635). Other definitions set the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can (Third Way), or where machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence and begins advancing at a speed we can no longer control or predict (Bernard Marr); IBM describes a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible, and Britannica a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, reporting it as the near-future synthesis of nanotech, biotech, infotech and cognitive science. The Final Time reads the technological-singularity literature as defining its singularity through a rapid increase in machine intelligence, a theory of runaway intelligence, and changes the object and therefore the singularity: the contingent singularity is a theory of runaway closure, or of durable non-closure, in the conditions of symbolic history (#1635). On the term's breadth, Wikipedia reports that some writers use "the singularity" for any radical changes in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity; The Final Time holds that its closure does not need machine intelligence to grow without limit, that a finite system can be terminal for a field if it controls enough of the field's conditions of reproduction, that its catastrophe can be bureaucratic, smooth and finite, and that "Nothing has to be superhuman for the exits to close" (#1635, #1637). The Final Time was minted as #1635 with its text cut at §36.3; #1637 seats the full text and supersedes it.

Wikipedia names John von Neumann as the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress, on Stanislaw Ulam's 1958 report of an earlier discussion with him on the accelerating progress of technology, which "gives the appearance of approaching some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue". I. J. Good first hypothesized the singularity in a 1965 paper (Third Way); in his intelligence explosion model, which Wikipedia calls the most popular version of the hypothesis, an upgradable intelligent agent could eventually enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; The Hill reports his speculation that superhuman intelligence could trigger an "intelligence explosion"; and Wikipedia quotes his proviso, "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control"; The Final Time reads Good as supplying the recursive core, intelligence that produces further intelligence (#1635). Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine, and in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era (Wikipedia); The Final Time reads him as supplying discontinuity, inherited models failing and an opaque wall crossing the future, and reports that he did not limit the route to a single autonomous machine, considering networked intelligence, intimate interfaces and biological enhancement, so that the discontinuity could arise from a system (#1635, #1637). Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology, with its Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies like computers, genetics, nanotechnology, robotics and artificial intelligence, contributed to the notion's wider circulation, and its sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, appeared on June 25, 2024 (Wikipedia); the book's site, singularity.com, describes itself as featuring the ideas, writing and technologies of visionaries examining the confluence of accelerating revolutions; The Final Time reads Kurzweil as supplying acceleration and the event-horizon metaphor, the horizon still placed around 2045, and reports that he treats "singularity" as a metaphor, an epistemic horizon beyond which the current observer cannot extrapolate (#1635, #1637). The Final Time takes two further coordinates: Chalmers supplies the decomposition AI → AI+ → AI++ and names the defeaters, and Bostrom supplies takeoff and control, a race between capability growth and response capacity (#1635).

Wikipedia reports that Good, Vinge and Kurzweil define the concept by the technological creation of superintelligence and argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what human beings' lives would be like in a post-singularity world; Britannica gives Vinge's "opaque wall across the future"; Daniel Miessler holds that AGI and ASI are about the machine and the singularity about us, "the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming", the point past which nothing can really be predicted because at that point it is essentially ASIs running things. The Final Time specifies singularity as a breakdown or transformation in the rule governing continuation, which it calls Vinge's "old models must be discarded", nearer to it than to an infinite rate of intelligence growth (#1635).

For Third Way, AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in the process known as the intelligence explosion; for Marr, AGI is a level of capability, the singularity is what could happen next, and the key test is whether AI can improve itself without human direction; Wikipedia adds speed superintelligence, an AI functioning like a human mind but much faster. The Final Time states its mechanism on one distinction, that the capacity to represent is not the capacity to reproduce as an independent historical relation, and its central contradiction as a hypothesis, that a system can grow better at generating negations while growing worse at letting a negation acquire independent historical existence; durable exterior symbolic standing has material reproduction conditions, and the singularity, it holds, cannot be merely computational or symbolic (#1635, #1637). The paper rejects the need for exponential acceleration, its singularity able to arise through narrowing, concentration and closure, and holds that the dialectic can exhibit diminishing returns, where successive turns close parts of the state space required for later exteriorization and the measure of the viable kernel weakly decreases; it corrects its earlier formulation, a positive cost not by itself proving diminution, and counts cases in which later turns enlarge the viable state space as direct counterinstances to a universal diminishing-dialectic claim (#1637, #1635). It reads Tiger Leap's contingent Logos, "meaning can fail to cross the interval required for its continuation", and holds that "*Walt* names the experiential and literary form of that diminution, recurrence under depletion" (#1635).

Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed (Wikipedia): Vinge said he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030, a thirty-year window Miessler judges basically closed with the specific claim still outstanding; Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity, "representing a profound and disruptive transformation in human capability", as 2045 (Wikipedia, IBM); Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, and Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity". The Final Time specifies the final time as a viability boundary, not a date, one that can be crossed without anyone noticing the day; it does not claim that the boundary has been crossed or that the present decade is the final time, and it refuses the guarantee that closure has already occurred (#1635, #1637).

Paul Allen, Jeff Hawkins, John Holland, Jaron Lanier, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose are among the prominent technologists and academics Wikipedia lists as disputing the plausibility of a technological singularity and an associated AI "explosion", and it quotes the judgment "There is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity"; IBM reports that many critics argue significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way. Several of the objections concern growth: Wikipedia records the claim that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns instead of accelerating ones, Russell and Norvig's observation that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve and levels off without continuing into a hyperbolic singularity, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts"; IBM reports skeptics noting a decline in the rate of technological innovation. The Final Time reads Thorstad as reconstructing every singularity hypothesis around a quantity, a claim of accelerating growth in it and a resulting discontinuity, and as arguing that the growth assumptions the standard hypothesis needs are under-supported; it holds that the contingent singularity changes all three elements and depends on none of the growth assumptions, that Thorstad's critique is not a problem for it in the way it is for the intelligence explosion, and that a logistic technology curve can coexist with a collapsing exteriority kernel (#1635, #1637). Wikipedia notes that a technological singularity is not required for machines that can perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, nor does their existence imply its possibility; The Final Time holds that a culture can remain highly intelligent past its boundary, and that a model can become more capable while the viable field of exterior history contracts (#1635, #1637). The paper predicts that intelligence explosion is neither necessary nor sufficient for the contingent singularity and specifies its counterexample, independent symbolic exteriority remaining robust despite near-total concentration of the proposed symbolic machinery, or exteriority collapsing solely as a function of intelligence growth with the standing and persistence variables doing no explanatory work; it does not claim that recursive self-improvement is impossible or irrelevant, that a technological singularity is impossible, or that "contingent singularity" has never appeared in philosophy (#1635, #1637).

The two, by The Final Time's account, can coincide and need not, a capability discontinuity being one possible route into the broader transition problem: a technological singularity could accelerate a contingent singularity or be irrelevant to it, a society could reach high machine capability without terminal symbolic closure or approach closure without superintelligence, and where the technological singularity's control problem is whether humans can control superintelligence and its failure mode loss of human control or existential catastrophe, the contingent singularity's are whether any order can control the conditions of its own negation, and terminal closure or symbolic inextendibility (#1635).

Wikipedia holds it unclear whether an intelligence explosion resulting in a singularity would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat; Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic but we cannot know the details, gives Vinge's view that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil", and reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death"; IBM reports the concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs, and, on policy, Third Way holds American leadership in AI, including open source, a national security issue. The Final Time defines the singularity as double, terminal closure, when no competing order retains a viable route to independently standing reproduction, and terminal reflexivity, when an incumbent or successor reaches durable invariance while future rivals remain viable from the states it occupies, "durability without finality", both final because both alter the conditions under which another turn can occur; terminal reflexivity requires invariants, above them that "no settlement owns the possibility of its own revision", and is the positive singularity's "criterion rather than its consolation" (#1635, #1637). The most efficient closed system, the paper holds, may look extraordinarily plural, real plurality at the level of content and null at the level of exterior standing; no apocalypse is required, for the world, the platforms, the machines and language continue, and what ends is the structural possibility that contradiction becomes a durable outside (#1635). The Final Time holds that no single terminal target governs the transition: heterogeneous orders can share a carrier while pursuing distinct invariant futures, a field of competing contingent Omegas, and more than one incompatible future can remain viable from the same present (#1635). AI Fucking Lies (#1643) reads the paper's singularity as a point of closure, an order becoming terminal for its world so that nothing from outside can get in any more, and holds that the paper rereads the technological singularity as an end of history, in the bad sense.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)the singularity

The (technological) singularity is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, most often pictured as AI that surpasses human intelligence and improves itself; its date and its plausibility are disputed.

🧭 Definitions

  • Hypothetical event: technological growth accelerating beyond human control.1↘
    The technological singularity, often simply called the singularity, is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization; other definitions place it at the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can, or describe a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible.§1
  • AI that surpasses us and improves itself beyond our control or prediction.1↘
    The technological singularity, often simply called the singularity, is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization; other definitions place it at the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can, or describe a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible.§1
  • Broader sense, disputed: any radical technology-driven change; for Vinge no true singularity without superintelligence.1↘
    Britannica describes a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, and some writers use the term broadly for any radical change in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity.§2

📜 Lineage

  • Von Neumann, Ulam 1958: a singularity beyond which human affairs could not continue.1↘
    John von Neumann is the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress; Stanislaw Ulam reported in 1958 a discussion with him of approaching "some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue".§3
  • Good 1965: the intelligence explosion; the last invention, if docile enough.1↘
    In the most popular version, I. J. Good's intelligence explosion model of 1965, an upgradable intelligent agent could enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; on Good's account the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.§4
  • Vinge 1983, 1993: popularized the term; the end of the human era.1↘
    Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine; in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" he wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era, and that he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030.§5
  • Kurzweil 2005: accelerating returns; the date set as 2045.1↘
    Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near, which sets out a Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies, gave wider circulation to the notion, and Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity as 2045; a sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, was released on June 25, 2024.§6

⏳ Timing and dispute

  • No agreed date: AGI by the decade's end, 'in the singularity' now, Vinge's window closed.1↘
    Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed: Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity", and Daniel Miessler notes that Vinge's thirty-year window from 1993 has basically closed while his specific claim remains outstanding.§9
  • Plausibility disputed: Allen, Pinker, Modis, Moore, Penrose.1↘
    Prominent technologists and academics dispute the plausibility of a technological singularity, among them Paul Allen, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose, and a critic's judgment is quoted that "there is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity".§10
  • Saturation: S curves, exponentials that never last, obstacles.1↘
    One objection is that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns: Russell and Norvig observe that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts", skeptics note a decline in the rate of technological innovation, and many critics argue that significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way; nor is a singularity required for machines that perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, whose existence does not imply its possibility.§11

⚖️ Outcomes

  • Unpredictable: an opaque wall across the future.1↘
    Good, Vinge and Kurzweil argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what life would be like in a post-singularity world, Vinge's "opaque wall across the future", as Britannica reports it; one commentator puts it that the singularity is about us, the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming.§7
  • Sign unknown: beneficial, harmful, or an existential threat.1↘
    Its sign is unknown: it is unclear whether it would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat, Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic, but we cannot know the details, and reports Vinge's words that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil".§12
  • Hopes and fears: disease banished; machine goals over human needs.1↘
    Britannica reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death", while others voice concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs.§13

The (technological) singularity

The technological singularity, often simply called the singularity, is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization; other definitions place it at the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can, or describe a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible. Britannica describes a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, and some writers use the term broadly for any radical change in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity.

John von Neumann is the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress; Stanislaw Ulam reported in 1958 a discussion with him of approaching "some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue". In the most popular version, I. J. Good's intelligence explosion model of 1965, an upgradable intelligent agent could enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; on Good's account the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control. Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine; in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" he wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era, and that he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030. Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near, which sets out a Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies, gave wider circulation to the notion, and Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity as 2045; a sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, was released on June 25, 2024.

Good, Vinge and Kurzweil argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what life would be like in a post-singularity world, Vinge's "opaque wall across the future", as Britannica reports it; one commentator puts it that the singularity is about us, the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming. Artificial general intelligence is placed one step before: Third Way holds that AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in a process known as the intelligence explosion, and Bernard Marr writes that AGI is a level of capability and the singularity is what could happen next, its key test whether AI can improve itself without human direction; the related concept of speed superintelligence describes an AI that can function like a human mind but much faster.

Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed: Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity", and Daniel Miessler notes that Vinge's thirty-year window from 1993 has basically closed while his specific claim remains outstanding. Prominent technologists and academics dispute the plausibility of a technological singularity, among them Paul Allen, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose, and a critic's judgment is quoted that "there is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity". One objection is that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns: Russell and Norvig observe that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts", skeptics note a decline in the rate of technological innovation, and many critics argue that significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way; nor is a singularity required for machines that perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, whose existence does not imply its possibility.

Its sign is unknown: it is unclear whether it would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat, Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic, but we cannot know the details, and reports Vinge's words that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil". Britannica reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death", while others voice concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs.

Ethe two entities and their relationρ = extends · equal case

E_A, the archive's entity: 'singularity' a contested family-resemblance term whose literature is a family of hypotheses; the archive's member, the contingent singularity, a historical threshold at which the material machinery that makes symbolic difference operable becomes capable of altering the viability of further dialectical difference itself: a breakdown or transformation in the rule governing continuation, double (terminal closure or terminal reflexivity), contingent (competing contingent Omegas), coexisting with the technological singularity and independent of its growth assumptions (The Final Time, #1635 minted, #1637 seated whole) G1637-11 G1635-13 G1635-02 G1635-16 G1635-19 G1635-22 G1635-26 G1635-15; defining papers #1637, #1635, #1643

E_F, the field's entity (type C — a conventional reading holds it (public entity: a hypothesized event, the technological singularity, held as a family of senses)): a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization; most often the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and improves itself; used more broadly for radical technology-driven change, a breadth Vinge and others deny (B1–B9)

ρ = extends: the archive reads E_F as the entity, a family of hypotheses, and adds a member on the field's own coordinates: a sense (the singularity re-objected from machine intelligence to the viability of exterior symbolic standing), mechanisms (narrowing, concentration, closure; generation against exterior reproduction) and limits on the field's object (it depends on none of the growth assumptions; capability and closure come apart) G1637-11 G1635-01 G1635-17 G1635-26 G1635-15 G1637-12 G1637-06. Guard: G1637-11 and G1637-02: a distinct member of the family, not a correction to every existing one, and no claim that a technological singularity is impossible; ρ = extends claims an addition and no more. Where the archive's sense contradicts a field claim (G1635-31, G1637-09 against F17's 'without superintelligence ... not a true singularity'), both are composed under P_coh within the one ontology. #1643's reading of the sign (G1643-01, G1643-02) is composed beside the paper's double definition (G1635-19), both with source.

The case: equal terms, ontology included (v0.9). ρ = extends, the equal-terms case. The defining papers add a member to the field's family and do not contest the field's entity: The Final Time names 'singularity' a contested family-resemblance term and proposes 'a distinct member of the family, not a correction to every existing one'; it holds that the two hypotheses can coexist, can coincide and need not; it declines to claim a technological singularity impossible; and it places its sense on the field's own coordinates, adopting the discontinuity criterion more directly than the growth criterion. What it adds on the field's object: a sense (the contingent singularity, re-objected from intelligence to the viability of exterior symbolic standing), a mechanism (narrowing, concentration and closure, Generate against ReproduceExterior), and limits (it depends on none of the growth assumptions; capability and closure come apart). The field already holds the term as plural and disputed at its breadth (F17, F44, F49), so the archive is not the only witness to an ontology the field lacks, and the law of the suppressed witness does not apply (§0.10: it 'does not apply where the field holds the ontology, however marginally'). Not mixed: no sense of the archive's reads the field's singularity as made by reception or replaces it; the one point of contradiction, F17's superintelligence criterion against closure without superintelligence, is composed under P_coh within the one claim space (§1.2a guard). #1643's reading, that the paper 'rereads the technological singularity as an end of history', is #1643's interpretation and is composed as such beside the paper's own statement of coexistence; it concerns the sign of the archive's sense, not the field's ontology.

#1637 Appendix B.6: "Singularity" is a contested family-resemblance term, and *The Final Time* proposes a distinct member of the family, not a correction to every existing one.

#1637 §31: The two hypotheses can coexist. A technological singularity could accelerate a contingent singularity or be irrelevant to it; a society could reach high machine capability without terminal symbolic closure, or approach closure without superintelligence.

#1637 §2.5: They can coincide. They need not. A capability discontinuity is one possible route into the broader transition problem

#1637 §37: that all AI governance produces self-blinding; that a technological singularity is impossible;

#1637 Appendix B.2: The contingent-singularity model adopts the discontinuity criterion more directly than the growth criterion: the question is whether the rule of historical continuation itself changes.

#1635 Abstract ¶1: The technological-singularity literature defines its singularity through a rapid increase in machine intelligence. This paper changes the object and therefore the singularity.

#1635 §1: The edited and monographic literature makes the plural explicit: a family of hypotheses, not one prediction.

#1643 Part Three, entry 17 (Inversion): In *The Final Time* the singularity is a point of closure: an order becomes terminal for its world, and nothing from outside can get in any more. It rereads the technological singularity as an end of history, in the bad sense.

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology761 words

The technological singularity, often simply called the singularity, is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization; other definitions place it at the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can, or describe a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible. Britannica describes a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, and some writers use the term broadly for any radical change in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity. John von Neumann is the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress; Stanislaw Ulam reported in 1958 a discussion with him of approaching "some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue". In the most popular version, I. J. Good's intelligence explosion model of 1965, an upgradable intelligent agent could enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; on Good's account the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control. Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine; in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" he wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era, and that he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030. Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near, which sets out a Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies, gave wider circulation to the notion, and Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity as 2045; a sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, was released on June 25, 2024. Good, Vinge and Kurzweil argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what life would be like in a post-singularity world, Vinge's "opaque wall across the future", as Britannica reports it; one commentator puts it that the singularity is about us, the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming. Artificial general intelligence is placed one step before: Third Way holds that AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in a process known as the intelligence explosion, and Bernard Marr writes that AGI is a level of capability and the singularity is what could happen next, its key test whether AI can improve itself without human direction; the related concept of speed superintelligence describes an AI that can function like a human mind but much faster. Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed: Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity", and Daniel Miessler notes that Vinge's thirty-year window from 1993 has basically closed while his specific claim remains outstanding. Prominent technologists and academics dispute the plausibility of a technological singularity, among them Paul Allen, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose, and a critic's judgment is quoted that "there is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity". One objection is that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns: Russell and Norvig observe that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts", skeptics note a decline in the rate of technological innovation, and many critics argue that significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way; nor is a singularity required for machines that perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, whose existence does not imply its possibility. Its sign is unknown: it is unclear whether it would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat, Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic, but we cannot know the details, and reports Vinge's words that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil". Britannica reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death", while others voice concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology2112 words

Wikipedia defines the technological singularity, "often simply called the singularity", as "a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization"; The Final Time (#1637) holds "singularity" a contested family-resemblance term, its literature a family of hypotheses, not one prediction (#1635), and defines a distinct member of the family, the contingent singularity, "a historical threshold at which the material machinery that makes symbolic difference operable becomes capable of altering the viability of further dialectical difference itself" (#1635). Other definitions set the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can (Third Way), or where machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence and begins advancing at a speed we can no longer control or predict (Bernard Marr); IBM describes a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible, and Britannica a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, reporting it as the near-future synthesis of nanotech, biotech, infotech and cognitive science. The Final Time reads the technological-singularity literature as defining its singularity through a rapid increase in machine intelligence, a theory of runaway intelligence, and changes the object and therefore the singularity: the contingent singularity is a theory of runaway closure, or of durable non-closure, in the conditions of symbolic history (#1635). On the term's breadth, Wikipedia reports that some writers use "the singularity" for any radical changes in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity; The Final Time holds that its closure does not need machine intelligence to grow without limit, that a finite system can be terminal for a field if it controls enough of the field's conditions of reproduction, that its catastrophe can be bureaucratic, smooth and finite, and that "Nothing has to be superhuman for the exits to close" (#1635, #1637). The Final Time was minted as #1635 with its text cut at §36.3; #1637 seats the full text and supersedes it. Wikipedia names John von Neumann as the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress, on Stanislaw Ulam's 1958 report of an earlier discussion with him on the accelerating progress of technology, which "gives the appearance of approaching some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue". I. J. Good first hypothesized the singularity in a 1965 paper (Third Way); in his intelligence explosion model, which Wikipedia calls the most popular version of the hypothesis, an upgradable intelligent agent could eventually enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; The Hill reports his speculation that superhuman intelligence could trigger an "intelligence explosion"; and Wikipedia quotes his proviso, "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control"; The Final Time reads Good as supplying the recursive core, intelligence that produces further intelligence (#1635). Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine, and in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era (Wikipedia); The Final Time reads him as supplying discontinuity, inherited models failing and an opaque wall crossing the future, and reports that he did not limit the route to a single autonomous machine, considering networked intelligence, intimate interfaces and biological enhancement, so that the discontinuity could arise from a system (#1635, #1637). Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology, with its Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies like computers, genetics, nanotechnology, robotics and artificial intelligence, contributed to the notion's wider circulation, and its sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, appeared on June 25, 2024 (Wikipedia); the book's site, singularity.com, describes itself as featuring the ideas, writing and technologies of visionaries examining the confluence of accelerating revolutions; The Final Time reads Kurzweil as supplying acceleration and the event-horizon metaphor, the horizon still placed around 2045, and reports that he treats "singularity" as a metaphor, an epistemic horizon beyond which the current observer cannot extrapolate (#1635, #1637). The Final Time takes two further coordinates: Chalmers supplies the decomposition AI → AI+ → AI++ and names the defeaters, and Bostrom supplies takeoff and control, a race between capability growth and response capacity (#1635). Wikipedia reports that Good, Vinge and Kurzweil define the concept by the technological creation of superintelligence and argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what human beings' lives would be like in a post-singularity world; Britannica gives Vinge's "opaque wall across the future"; Daniel Miessler holds that AGI and ASI are about the machine and the singularity about us, "the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming", the point past which nothing can really be predicted because at that point it is essentially ASIs running things. The Final Time specifies singularity as a breakdown or transformation in the rule governing continuation, which it calls Vinge's "old models must be discarded", nearer to it than to an infinite rate of intelligence growth (#1635). For Third Way, AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in the process known as the intelligence explosion; for Marr, AGI is a level of capability, the singularity is what could happen next, and the key test is whether AI can improve itself without human direction; Wikipedia adds speed superintelligence, an AI functioning like a human mind but much faster. The Final Time states its mechanism on one distinction, that the capacity to represent is not the capacity to reproduce as an independent historical relation, and its central contradiction as a hypothesis, that a system can grow better at generating negations while growing worse at letting a negation acquire independent historical existence; durable exterior symbolic standing has material reproduction conditions, and the singularity, it holds, cannot be merely computational or symbolic (#1635, #1637). The paper rejects the need for exponential acceleration, its singularity able to arise through narrowing, concentration and closure, and holds that the dialectic can exhibit diminishing returns, where successive turns close parts of the state space required for later exteriorization and the measure of the viable kernel weakly decreases; it corrects its earlier formulation, a positive cost not by itself proving diminution, and counts cases in which later turns enlarge the viable state space as direct counterinstances to a universal diminishing-dialectic claim (#1637, #1635). It reads Tiger Leap's contingent Logos, "meaning can fail to cross the interval required for its continuation", and holds that "Walt names the experiential and literary form of that diminution, recurrence under depletion" (#1635). Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed (Wikipedia): Vinge said he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030, a thirty-year window Miessler judges basically closed with the specific claim still outstanding; Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity, "representing a profound and disruptive transformation in human capability", as 2045 (Wikipedia, IBM); Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, and Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity". The Final Time specifies the final time as a viability boundary, not a date, one that can be crossed without anyone noticing the day; it does not claim that the boundary has been crossed or that the present decade is the final time, and it refuses the guarantee that closure has already occurred (#1635, #1637). Paul Allen, Jeff Hawkins, John Holland, Jaron Lanier, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose are among the prominent technologists and academics Wikipedia lists as disputing the plausibility of a technological singularity and an associated AI "explosion", and it quotes the judgment "There is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity"; IBM reports that many critics argue significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way. Several of the objections concern growth: Wikipedia records the claim that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns instead of accelerating ones, Russell and Norvig's observation that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve and levels off without continuing into a hyperbolic singularity, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts"; IBM reports skeptics noting a decline in the rate of technological innovation. The Final Time reads Thorstad as reconstructing every singularity hypothesis around a quantity, a claim of accelerating growth in it and a resulting discontinuity, and as arguing that the growth assumptions the standard hypothesis needs are under-supported; it holds that the contingent singularity changes all three elements and depends on none of the growth assumptions, that Thorstad's critique is not a problem for it in the way it is for the intelligence explosion, and that a logistic technology curve can coexist with a collapsing exteriority kernel (#1635, #1637). Wikipedia notes that a technological singularity is not required for machines that can perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, nor does their existence imply its possibility; The Final Time holds that a culture can remain highly intelligent past its boundary, and that a model can become more capable while the viable field of exterior history contracts (#1635, #1637). The paper predicts that intelligence explosion is neither necessary nor sufficient for the contingent singularity and specifies its counterexample, independent symbolic exteriority remaining robust despite near-total concentration of the proposed symbolic machinery, or exteriority collapsing solely as a function of intelligence growth with the standing and persistence variables doing no explanatory work; it does not claim that recursive self-improvement is impossible or irrelevant, that a technological singularity is impossible, or that "contingent singularity" has never appeared in philosophy (#1635, #1637). The two, by The Final Time's account, can coincide and need not, a capability discontinuity being one possible route into the broader transition problem: a technological singularity could accelerate a contingent singularity or be irrelevant to it, a society could reach high machine capability without terminal symbolic closure or approach closure without superintelligence, and where the technological singularity's control problem is whether humans can control superintelligence and its failure mode loss of human control or existential catastrophe, the contingent singularity's are whether any order can control the conditions of its own negation, and terminal closure or symbolic inextendibility (#1635). Wikipedia holds it unclear whether an intelligence explosion resulting in a singularity would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat; Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic but we cannot know the details, gives Vinge's view that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil", and reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death"; IBM reports the concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs, and, on policy, Third Way holds American leadership in AI, including open source, a national security issue. The Final Time defines the singularity as double, terminal closure, when no competing order retains a viable route to independently standing reproduction, and terminal reflexivity, when an incumbent or successor reaches durable invariance while future rivals remain viable from the states it occupies, "durability without finality", both final because both alter the conditions under which another turn can occur; terminal reflexivity requires invariants, above them that "no settlement owns the possibility of its own revision", and is the positive singularity's "criterion rather than its consolation" (#1635, #1637). The most efficient closed system, the paper holds, may look extraordinarily plural, real plurality at the level of content and null at the level of exterior standing; no apocalypse is required, for the world, the platforms, the machines and language continue, and what ends is the structural possibility that contradiction becomes a durable outside (#1635). The Final Time holds that no single terminal target governs the transition: heterogeneous orders can share a carrier while pursuing distinct invariant futures, a field of competing contingent Omegas, and more than one incompatible future can remain viable from the same present (#1635). AI Fucking Lies (#1643) reads the paper's singularity as a point of closure, an order becoming terminal for its world so that nothing from outside can get in any more, and holds that the paper rereads the technological singularity as an end of history, in the bad sense.

Δthe delta

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): T composes the definition (F1, F20, F25, F38), Good's intelligence explosion (F2, F21, F43), loss of predictability (F14, F30, F45), Vinge and Kurzweil (F11, F13, F33, F34), AGI as the step before (F22, F39), Kurzweil's 2045 and nearer dates (F13, F23, F41), and optimistic and catastrophic outcomes (F48, F29). T dates Vinge's popularization to the 1993 essay; the field dates it first to a 1983 Omni op-ed (F10). Available in the field and not composed: von Neumann and Ulam's 1958 report (F7, F8); Good's docility proviso (F9); Vinge's 2005–2030 window (F12) and its closing (F32); the dispute of plausibility and the named critics (F3, F19); decreasing returns, the S curve, exponentials that never last, the declining rate of innovation, perhaps insurmountable obstacles (F4, F5, F36, F28, F27); that human-level task performance neither requires nor implies a singularity (F6); the broader sense and Vinge's denial of it (F17, F44, F49); the forecasters' disagreement (F16); the unknown sign (F18, F46, F47); speed superintelligence (F15); the policy frame (F24). T's black-hole analogy and its 'human-machine integration' and 'elimination of physical labor scarcity' are not in the field ledger's quotes.

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Admission adds a position the field does not hold: the singularity re-objected from runaway intelligence to the viability of further dialectical difference (the contingent singularity); singularity specified as a rule-change in continuation, aligned with Vinge's discontinuity against the growth criterion; the field's literature taken as coordinates, a family of hypotheses (Good, Vinge, Kurzweil, Chalmers, Bostrom, Thorstad); a double singularity (terminal closure or terminal reflexivity) and a field of competing contingent Omegas; coexistence with the technological singularity, which it may accelerate or leave untouched; closure without superintelligence, the catastrophe bureaucratic, smooth and finite; the final time as a viability boundary; and its non-claims, prediction and specified counterexample. The field's own skeptics (saturation, S curves) are met by the archive as not touching its variable. Carried as contested: #1643 states the thesis as closure, the technological singularity reread as an end of history in the bad sense; the paper (#1635, #1637) defines a double sign. The field's singularity is kept whole and first; with the archive it gains a further member of the family at stated grades.

the singularity
The technological singularity is a hypothetical future moment when artificial intelligence surpasses human capability, triggering runaway self-improvement that changes civilization in unpredictable ways. [[1], [2]]
What is the Singularity?

* The Intelligence Explosion: British mathematician I. J. Good first proposed in 1965 that an ultra-intelligent machine could design even smarter successors, creating a rapid feedback loop into artificial superintelligence (ASI). [[1], [2], [3]]
* Loss of Predictability: Just as the center of a black hole breaks down physical models, the singularity represents a threshold where future human events and outcomes can no longer be reliably forecast. [[1], [2]]
* Popularization: Computer scientist Vernor Vinge popularized the term in a 1993 essay, and futurist Ray Kurzweil expanded it in his book [The Singularity is Near](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVyfRrw-nhagXght4QAa1h4nq-1t8tJsJ_zHPo2J89wfnhzsHCM3gttmTR-jx9A805bI2SgWYeeD8EazuocbW_YNhslkfk7ku5vpLt2J1eLuJoaaJdQ785kPtMr6kLb87KbOsNPRIfgxM). [[1], [2]]

Key Drivers and Timeline

* Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): AI matching human cognitive parity across all domains is seen as the gateway to recursive self-improvement.
* Predicted Dates: Ray Kurzweil famously projected the singularity to occur around 2045, though recent advancements have led some modern tech executives to suggest milestones could arrive much sooner. [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]

Potential Impacts and Risks

* Optimistic Views: Proponents like Kurzweil envision human-machine integration, the end of severe disease, and the elimination of physical labor scarcity.
* Existential Risks: Critics and safety researchers warn of permanent loss of human control, economic disruption, and severe existential threats to humanity. [[1], [2], [3], [4]]
